case.title: The Beacon Goes Dark
case.central_mystery: Thomas Ashby, the owner-editor of the town's only newspaper, is found drowned at the base of the old town dock, in a spot he was known to frequent alone at night for his research. Everything about the scene says accident - except the man never went anywhere without his phone, his recorder, and a locked satchel of notes, and none of the three were ever found. There is no camera footage of his death. No fingerprints survive a body pulled from tidal water. No weapon is ever recovered. There is, in fact, no direct evidence of murder at all - only a slow accumulation of things that don't quite add up, in a town where almost everyone is hiding something, and only one of those somethings is the reason Tom Ashby died.
case.design_intent: This case is built to be solved through pattern, timeline, and elimination rather than a single decisive forensic hit. There is no confession, no matching fingerprint, no clean DNA trace, and no camera that catches the killer. The murder weapon (a smooth, fist-sized river stone) is functionally unrecoverable and forensically anonymous. The case must be broken by cross-referencing tide science, phone metadata, financial records, and one small, unguarded slip made by the killer during casual conversation - a detail about the scene that was never publicly released. AT LEAST FOUR of the six suspects should remain independently plausible as the killer for the majority of the investigation. The killer should be the suspect the player is least primed to suspect: a widely trusted, low-conflict community figure who appears throughout mainly in a helpful, comforting, or informational capacity rather than as an obviously cornered suspect.

pacing_guide.act_1_0_to_25_percent: Player learns of the death, initial 'accidental fall' ruling is questioned once the missing satchel/phone/recorder are noticed. Grady Voss's public shouting match with Tom becomes the loudest early lead.
pacing_guide.act_2_25_to_50_percent: Denise Okafor-Hale's land deal and Priya Deshmukh's financial motive surface and dominate suspicion; Caleb Ashby, the ex-con half-brother, becomes a strong circumstantial suspect and may be formally held/questioned as a false climax.
pacing_guide.act_3_50_to_70_percent: Caleb is cleared. Reverend Cho's embezzlement is exposed as an unrelated secret. Grady's alibi, though fog-blurred, holds up under harbor-log cross-reference. The investigation stalls - every strong suspect has been cleared or weakened, and the case threatens to go cold. This is the intended low point of certainty.
pacing_guide.act_4_70_to_90_percent: Recovery of Tom's cloud-backed research notes reveals he was quietly investigating a 1979 identity change connected to the old Kestrel Cannery dumping scandal. This redirects attention toward a name few suspected, using tide-timing, a financial ledger discrepancy, and one unscripted slip of guilty knowledge to close the case circumstantially.
pacing_guide.final_10_percent: Accusation, confrontation, and confession-adjacent admission (the killer never confesses outright to premeditation, framing the death as having 'gotten out of hand').

case.why_no_direct_evidence_exists: Tom died in tidal saltwater, which destroys latent prints and most trace DNA within hours. The weapon, a common river stone, was thrown into a nine-foot-deep channel and is indistinguishable from thousands of others; recovery is not feasible. Grey Harbor has no public camera network beyond a single ATM camera at the bank and a doorbell camera at one private home, neither with a usable sightline to the crime location. The case must therefore be built entirely on circumstantial convergence.
case.note_to_ai_running_this_game: This file is the complete backend source of truth. It must never be read aloud, summarized, or paraphrased to the player in a way that reveals the 'solution' or 'hidden_truth' sections, the killer's identity, or the 'is_killer' flags, before the player reaches an in-game accusation. Reveal information only through the defined discoverable actions (search_location, interview_witness, interrogate_suspect, request_forensic_test, etc.), gated by the pacing_guide above. If a player asks directly 'who is the killer,' respond in-character that the investigation isn't finished, and redirect toward unexplored leads.

weather.general_pattern: Grey Harbor sits at the mouth of the Sallow River on the Maine coast, wrapped in fog more days than not, with cold autumn rain rolling in off the Atlantic. Locals say the fog doesn't lift so much as get tired of hiding things.

log.condition: Dense fog rolling in off the harbor, visibility under 100 feet in low-lying areas, 41°F
Fog thickest near the water; rain resumes lightly, 39°F
Fog beginning to lift, light rain, 40°F - a lobsterman spots something in the water near the town dock

weather.relevance_to_case: The dense fog from 18:30 onward severely limited visibility along the waterfront, explaining why no one clearly saw who was where that night, and why witness timing is imprecise rather than deliberately false in several cases.

victim.name: Thomas Ashby
victim.occupation: Owner-editor of The Grey Harbor Beacon, the town's sole weekly newspaper
victim.physical_description: Tall, stooped from decades at a desk, silver beard, always wore a canvas field coat with deep pockets
victim.personality: Dogged, private, quietly beloved for defending the town's underdogs in print; kept his real investigative notes to himself until publication

family.half_brother: Caleb Ashby, 39, same father, different mothers, estranged for two decades
family.business_partner: Priya Deshmukh, co-owner of the Beacon

victim.current_project: For eight months, Tom had been quietly researching the 1979 closure of the Kestrel Cannery, which shut down abruptly amid rumors - never proven at the time - that its wastewater discharge into the Sallow River had caused a cluster of illnesses among families living along the tidal flats. He had recently begun requesting old county identity and property records, and had told his business partner only that he had 'one more thread to pull' before publication.
victim.last_seen_alive: 2025-11-03, approximately 18:50, driving his own car north out of town toward the old cannery access road
victim.missing_items: His phone, his digital voice recorder, and a locked leather satchel containing his physical research notes were never recovered, though his car was later found parked at the town dock, a location he was known to frequent for late-night writing.

solution.role_cover: Church organist at St. Brendan's and longtime director of the Grey Harbor Community Pantry, one of the town's most trusted and well-liked residents
solution.true_identity: Born Warren Pelletier, son of Arnold Pelletier, the Kestrel Cannery's plant supervisor in 1979, who oversaw the illegal wastewater discharge and quietly relocated the family out of state after a confidential settlement with several affected families avoided a public lawsuit. Warren returned to Grey Harbor under his mother's maiden name, Pell, in 1994, and rebuilt himself as a pillar of the community.
solution.true_motive: For three decades, Warren has personally administered a private, undisclosed 'relief fund' - money from the original 1979 settlement, which he inherited control of after his parents died - making small, quiet cash payments to the aging tidal-flat families still dealing with illness, on the condition they never discuss its source. In practice this let him monitor and suppress the story indefinitely while diverting a significant portion of the fund's interest for his own use over the years, effectively defrauding the very people it was meant to help. Tom Ashby's research into the 1979 name-change records and old cannery employment files was on the verge of exposing both the original cover-up and Warren's decades of quiet, ongoing fraud - the second discovery being, for Warren, by far the more urgent and personally ruinous threat, since it would end not just his father's reputation but his own life's work of trusted community standing, very possibly along with criminal fraud charges.
solution.how_it_happened: Using a prepaid phone Tom did not recognize, Warren anonymously contacted Tom two days before his death, claiming to have original 1979 cannery documents to hand over in person, and arranged a meeting at the old cannery outflow dock after dark, away from town. Warren, whom Tom trusted as the mild-mannered pantry director and had no reason to suspect, waited at the outflow dock. When Tom arrived and it became clear Tom already had enough information to identify Warren's real family connection regardless of any documents offered, a struggle broke out over Tom's satchel. Warren struck Tom once with a large, smooth river stone from the shoreline. Tom fell, unconscious but still breathing, into the tidal channel and drowned before Warren intervened further - a killing that was violent and deliberate in its opening act, though its fatal conclusion unfolded partly through inaction rather than a second blow. Warren took Tom's phone, recorder, and satchel, drove Tom's own car (using Tom's keys, taken from his coat) to the town dock to stage the more familiar 'he fell during his usual nighttime writing' scenario, wiped the interior surfaces he had touched, and discarded the stone into the deep channel off the outflow dock. He then returned on foot roughly a mile along the shore road to where he had left his own pantry delivery van, which a resident later recalled seeing near the outflow road that evening and assumed was simply Warren's routine surplus-food delivery run to the tidal-flat trailer park.
solution.weapon: A common, smooth, fist-sized river stone from the shoreline, discarded into a nine-foot-deep tidal channel and never recovered
solution.why_no_direct_evidence_exists_for_this_s: The stone weapon is unrecoverable and, even if found, would carry no unique forensic signature after hours in saltwater. Warren left no camera trail (no camera covers the outflow road). His fingerprints in Tom's car would be unremarkable even if found, since Warren occasionally rode with Tom on pantry-related errands in the past, giving him an innocent explanation for any trace that might theoretically survive. The case must be built entirely from: tide/algae-line evidence proving the body entered the water at the outflow, not the town dock; phone-tower and burner-phone metadata connecting the anonymous meeting request to a prepaid phone purchased in a nearby town; financial records showing decades of relief-fund fraud; a name-change and old employment record connecting 'Warren Pell' to 'Warren Pelletier'; and one unscripted verbal slip in which Warren describes a detail of how Tom 'must have hit his head on the dock pilings' - a specific, never-publicly-released detail about the (false) staged scene that only the person who staged it should have been able to state with such casual confidence before the medical examiner's report was released.
key_proof_chain: Tide charts and algae/mud staining on the body's clothing show it entered the water at the cannery outflow, roughly a mile from where Tom's car was found at the town dock - proving the 'died where his car was found' theory is false and someone moved the vehicle after the fact.

The autopsy identifies a curved, smooth-surfaced skull contusion inconsistent with the dock pilings (square-edged timber) at the town dock and inconsistent with any structure at the outflow dock either - consistent instead with a handheld rounded object, ruling out a simple fall at both locations.
Cell tower data places Tom's last phone activity (before it went permanently dark) pinging a tower consistent with the cannery outflow road at 18:55, not the town dock.

A burner phone, purchased with cash at a convenience store in the neighboring town of Aldermere three days before the murder, is traced via the store's till receipt and a partial description from the clerk; the number matches an anonymous call placed to Tom's phone the day before his death.

Financial audit of the 'Tidal Families Relief Fund,' privately administered by Warren Pell with no oversight board, shows consistent underpayment to beneficiary families relative to the fund's known original principal and reasonable interest growth over 30 years - money unaccounted for.

A 1994 legal name-change filing recovered from county records shows Warren Pelletier becoming Warren Pell, cross-referenced with a 1979 Kestrel Cannery employee badge photo of a teenage Warren Pelletier, matched to Warren Pell via a forensic age-progression/facial-comparison analysis.

Warren's own remark, made casually to a sheriff's deputy during an informal conversation before the medical examiner's report was public, that Tom 'must have hit his head on the dock pilings' - a detail no released statement had mentioned, and which does not match either actual death scene.

A neighbor's recollection of Warren's distinctive pantry delivery van parked near the cannery outflow road the evening of the murder, initially assumed innocuous, becomes significant only once cross-referenced against the tide/cell-tower timeline.
solution.how_case_is_broken: No single piece of evidence is sufficient alone. The investigation must first exhaust and eliminate the louder, more obvious suspects (Grady's temper, Denise's land deal, Priya's finances, Caleb's record, Reverend Cho's embezzlement) through alibi verification, at which point the case appears to stall. The breakthrough comes from re-examining the discovery scene itself rather than the suspects: the tide-chart and algae-staining mismatch proves the town dock was staged, which reopens the entire geography of the crime and points to the isolated cannery outflow instead. From there, cell-tower data anchors Tom there at 18:55, the burner-phone trail explains why he went there voluntarily, and the county name-change records - found only because Tom's own recovered research notes pointed investigators toward the 1979 employment files in the first place - identify Warren Pelletier/Pell as the only person with both a personal connection to the cannery scandal and control of the relief fund Tom was circling. His unscripted slip about the dock pilings, combined with the financial fraud in the fund he solely administers, closes the loop without ever requiring the murder weapon or a fingerprint.

suspects.name: Grady Voss
suspects.role: Lobsterman, third-generation, works the tidal flats near the old cannery
suspects.relationship_to_victim: Public shouting match with Tom one week before his death, witnessed by several people outside Moss's Diner, over Tom's forthcoming article implying contamination in Grady's traditional fishing grounds
suspects.personality: Blunt, quick-tempered, fiercely protective of his family's livelihood and reputation
suspects.motive_on_paper: Feared the article would destroy his business even if the contamination claims were decades old and unproven for his specific grounds; was overheard saying 'if that story runs, I'll make sure it's the last thing he writes'
suspects.secret: Has been selling a portion of his daily catch off the books to avoid reporting reduced-quota income to his ex-wife's child support calculation - an unrelated financial concealment
suspects.alibi_claim: Was out on his boat with a deckhand from 17:00 to nearly midnight, running a late set of traps before a forecasted storm
suspects.alibi_evidence: Harbor departure/return log and independent deckhand corroboration place him on the water for the relevant window, though the exact minute of return is fog-blurred and imprecise enough to sustain suspicion for a long stretch of the investigation before being effectively confirmed

suspects.name: Denise Okafor-Hale
suspects.role: Grey Harbor Select Board chair, pushing a redevelopment deal to convert the old cannery site into a private marina
suspects.relationship_to_victim: Tom's forthcoming article threatened to derail the redevelopment deal by reviving the contamination history, which could trigger a costly environmental review
suspects.personality: Polished, controlled, publicly warm but privately calculating
suspects.motive_on_paper: Quietly purchased land upstream of the proposed marina under a shell LLC, positioned to profit enormously if the redevelopment proceeds, and stood to lose that investment if Tom's article stalled the project
suspects.secret: The undisclosed land purchase and a conflict-of-interest violation of Select Board ethics rules
suspects.alibi_claim: States she was at a public Select Board budget meeting until 21:00
suspects.alibi_evidence: Confirmed false in the strict sense of her account - meeting minutes and five attendees confirm she left early, around 19:15, but her actual destination (a private meeting with the marina developer's financiers to finalize financing terms, at a restaurant in Aldermere, confirmed by a credit card receipt timestamped 19:40 and a hostess's recollection) has nothing to do with the murder and merely explains her evasiveness about the meeting's early end

suspects.name: Reverend Elias Cho
suspects.relationship_to_victim: Publicly clashed with Tom after the Beacon ran a small item about the pastor's estranged adult son's arrest in a neighboring county; accused Tom of unnecessary cruelty toward his family
suspects.personality: Warm in public, privately anxious and financially overextended
suspects.motive_on_paper: Resentment over the article and a fear that Tom's larger cannery piece would somehow further embarrass the church, whose original land donation from the Pelletier family decades ago is a matter of some discomfort locally
suspects.secret: Quietly used undesignated church discretionary funds, without full vestry approval, to post bail and hire a lawyer for his son - a financial impropriety unrelated to the murder
suspects.alibi_claim: Initially claims he was at the church preparing Sunday materials alone all evening
suspects.alibi_evidence: Actually drove to a county lockup ninety minutes away to see his son and arrange bail, confirmed by the jail's visitor log timestamped 19:05-20:20 that night, which he only admits once confronted, having lied purely to avoid revealing his son's situation and his own financial impropriety

suspects.name: Priya Deshmukh
suspects.role: Co-owner of The Grey Harbor Beacon, Tom's business partner for eleven years
suspects.relationship_to_victim: Close professional partnership strained in its final year by disagreement over the paper's finances
suspects.personality: Pragmatic, guarded, exhausted from years of propping up a failing small business
suspects.motive_on_paper: The Beacon was deeply in debt; Priya had been quietly negotiating with a regional media company to sell the paper, a deal Tom flatly refused, and Tom's death would leave her as sole owner free to sell without his objection, alongside a modest key-person life insurance policy on him the paper carried
suspects.secret: Had continued sale negotiations behind Tom's back after his refusal, technically a breach of their partnership agreement, unrelated to his death
suspects.alibi_claim: States she was visiting her elderly mother at Harborview Community Hospital that evening
suspects.alibi_evidence: Confirmed true - hospital visitor sign-in log and a nurse's independent recollection place her there from 18:00 to nearly 22:30

suspects.name: Caleb Ashby
suspects.role: Tom's estranged half-brother, recently returned to Grey Harbor after years away, currently unemployed
suspects.relationship_to_victim: Estranged for two decades; recently reappeared seeking a share of a small piece of inherited family property Tom had been managing, leading to a tense confrontation witnessed by a neighbor
suspects.personality: Defensive, evasive, carries a prior record for minor theft and one assault charge from years ago
suspects.motive_on_paper: Financial desperation and resentment; the most circumstantially 'obvious' suspect given his record and the recent inheritance dispute, making him a strong candidate for a false mid-investigation arrest
suspects.secret: Has been secretly sleeping in the abandoned family cabin on the disputed property without permission or utilities, and briefly poached from a neighbor's lobster pots to eat, both minor and unrelated to the murder, which is why he was cagey and evasive under initial questioning
suspects.alibi_claim: Initially refuses to say where he was, fueling suspicion
suspects.alibi_evidence: Eventually admits he was at the family cabin all night, which is corroborated once investigators find fresh signs of recent, repeated occupancy (a still-warm woodstove noted by a responding deputy checking the property two days later, and a store clerk in a nearby town who recalls him buying canned goods with exact-change cash that same evening at 19:30, timestamped by the till receipt, placing him well outside Grey Harbor at the relevant window)

suspects.name: Warren Pell
suspects.role: Church organist at St. Brendan's and director of the Grey Harbor Community Pantry
suspects.relationship_to_victim: Warmly regarded acquaintance; occasionally assisted Tom with community-outreach errands for the pantry, and was seen by others as a helpful, informational town-history source, including for Tom's own research
suspects.personality: Gentle, soft-spoken, endlessly patient, the kind of person other suspects and witnesses instinctively trust and confide in
suspects.motive_on_paper: None visible at first - appears to be simply a helpful bystander with no conflict with Tom whatsoever; his surface-level 'secret,' when it surfaces, initially seems to fully explain his nervousness without implicating him in murder
suspects.secret_surface_layer: Has been quietly taking small amounts from the community pantry's general donation box to help cover his wife's mounting prescription costs, a sympathetic, minor theft unrelated on its face to Tom's death - a red herring within the killer designed to feel like a satisfying, complete answer if discovered before the deeper layer
suspects.secret_true_layer: Is the son of the Kestrel Cannery's 1979 plant supervisor, changed his name from Pelletier to his mother's maiden name Pell in 1994, and has for three decades privately and secretly administered - and substantially defrauded - a hush-money 'relief fund' paid to affected tidal-flat families as part of the original 1979 settlement, using it to monitor and suppress the story indefinitely
suspects.alibi_claim: States he spent the evening alone at the church, preparing hymn selections and cleaning the organ pipes for Sunday service
suspects.alibi_evidence: Entirely unverifiable - no one else was at the church that evening, and his account is never directly contradicted by any witness in the early investigation, allowing him to remain unsuspicious far longer than any other suspect; only later does a neighbor's recollection of his pantry van near the cannery outflow road become significant once cross-referenced against the true crime-scene geography

witnesses.name: Marla Osei
witnesses.statement: Describes the public argument between Grady Voss and Tom Ashby a week before the murder, including Grady's exact words about it being 'the last thing he writes.'
witnesses.reliability: High, though the remark is later understood to be an angry exaggeration rather than a genuine threat, once Grady's alibi holds

witnesses.name: Deckhand Ollie Frank
witnesses.statement: Confirms being out on the water with Grady from roughly 17:00 until close to midnight, though admits the fog made it hard to be precise about exact return timing
witnesses.reliability: High, corroborated independently by the harbor departure/return log

witnesses.name: Select Board Clerk Naomi Griggs
witnesses.statement: Confirms Denise Okafor-Hale left the budget meeting early, around 19:15, without explanation
witnesses.reliability: High - official meeting minutes support this

witnesses.name: Hostess Renata Cole
witnesses.role: Works at a restaurant in Aldermere
witnesses.statement: Recalls seating Denise Okafor-Hale and two men in business attire at 19:35 that evening
witnesses.reliability: Moderate-high, corroborated by a credit card receipt

witnesses.name: Deputy Warden at the County Lockup
witnesses.statement: Confirms Reverend Elias Cho's visit from 19:05 to 20:20 that night

witnesses.name: Nurse Faye Delgado
witnesses.role: Works the evening shift at Harborview Community Hospital
witnesses.statement: Confirms Priya Deshmukh was present visiting her mother from roughly 18:00 to nearly 22:30
witnesses.reliability: High - independently corroborated by the hospital's visitor sign-in system

witnesses.name: Store Clerk Benny Trask
witnesses.role: Works the general store in the small town near the Ashby family cabin
witnesses.statement: Recalls Caleb Ashby buying canned goods with exact cash at 19:30 that evening
witnesses.reliability: High - till receipt timestamp confirms it

witnesses.name: Deputy Ronald Pike
witnesses.role: Responding deputy who checked the disputed family property two days after the murder
witnesses.statement: Notes signs of recent, repeated occupancy at the cabin, including a still-faintly-warm woodstove

witnesses.name: Lobsterman Hollis Baird
witnesses.role: Found the body the morning of November 4th
witnesses.statement: Describes spotting Tom's body caught against pilings near the town dock at dawn

witnesses.name: Neighbor Ida Marsh
witnesses.role: Lives along the cannery outflow road, near the tidal-flat trailer park
witnesses.statement: Recalls seeing the community pantry's distinctive van parked near the outflow road sometime in the early evening of November 3rd, and assumed it was a routine surplus-food delivery, as Warren Pell made such runs regularly
witnesses.truthfulness: Truthful, but her account is initially treated as trivial background color rather than a lead
witnesses.reliability: Moderate - her sense of the exact time is vague ('sometime before full dark'), but becomes significant once cross-referenced with the tide/cell-tower timeline much later in the investigation

witnesses.name: Convenience Store Clerk in Aldermere
witnesses.role: Sold a prepaid burner phone three days before the murder
witnesses.statement: Recalls an older male customer paying cash for a prepaid phone, but cannot confidently identify him from a photo lineup beyond general build and age range
witnesses.reliability: Low-to-moderate on identification, high on the transaction record itself, which is what ultimately matters

witnesses.name: Deputy Sarah Kwan
witnesses.role: Responding deputy, present during an informal conversation with Warren Pell days before the medical examiner's report was released
witnesses.statement: Recalls Warren remarking, unprompted, that Tom 'must have hit his head on the dock pilings' - a detail she initially thought nothing of, since it seemed like reasonable townsfolk speculation
witnesses.reliability: High once its significance is recognized - this detail was never part of any public statement, official release, or town rumor mill traced back to any other source

vehicles.relevant_movement: Left his house at approximately 18:50; later found parked at the town dock, though cell-tower and tide evidence eventually show he was actually at the cannery outflow, roughly a mile away, meaning the car was moved after his death

vehicles.vehicle: Grey Harbor Community Pantry delivery van, white with a hand-painted logo
vehicles.relevant_movement: Recalled by a neighbor (Ida Marsh) near the cannery outflow road in the early evening of November 3rd, initially assumed to be a routine delivery
Departed the harbor at 17:00, returned close to midnight per the harbor log
Drove to Aldermere after leaving the Select Board meeting early, arriving at the restaurant by 19:35
Drove to the county lockup, arriving 19:05, per the visitor log

vehicles.vehicle: None currently - travels on foot or borrows rides
vehicles.relevant_movement: Walked to the general store near the family cabin at 19:30 per the till receipt

cctv.footage: Covers only the bank's own small parking lot; shows nothing relevant to the case

cctv.camera: Private doorbell camera, Corbin residence on Elm Street
cctv.footage: Faces only the Corbin family's own front porch, well away from any relevant location

cctv.camera: None covering the town dock or the cannery outflow road
cctv.footage: No camera coverage exists at either location, which is precisely why the case hinges on tide science, cell data, and testimony rather than footage

Tom tells Priya he has 'one more thread to pull' and will explain everything once he's sure, and not to expect him back at the office until late

messages.text: Heading out. If this checks out, we run it Thursday. Trust me on this one.
You know that land is half mine. I'm not going anywhere this time.

emails.content_summary: Confirms a private dinner meeting to finalize financing terms for the marina redevelopment, scheduling it for the evening of November 3rd - unrelated to the murder but explaining her whereabouts

A working outline for the planned article, noting 'name change filed 1994 - confirm connection to 1979 supervisor' and 'relief fund - who actually controls it now? follow the money forward, not just back' - recovered later from his cloud backup since his physical notes and phone were taken

bank_records.relevance: Core financial proof of Warren's true motive, discoverable only once his real identity connects him to fund administration

bank_records.transaction: Modest but unexplained supplemental deposits over many years, inconsistent with his modest known income from part-time music instruction and a small pension
bank_records.purpose_established: Personal benefit from the diverted relief fund
bank_records.relevance: Corroborates the fund fraud once the fund itself is audited

locations.name: Town Dock (Grey Harbor waterfront)
locations.description: A weathered municipal dock where fishing boats tie up and where Tom Ashby was known to sit alone at night writing in his car or on a bench, headphones in, working through drafts. His car was found parked here the morning after his death.
possible_tests: Comparison of dock piling shape/material to the skull wound
hidden_items: Absence of Tom's phone, recorder, and satchel from the car - a negative clue
No mud/algae staining on the car's floor mats consistent with someone soaked from the water having driven it, suggesting someone else drove it here afterward
locations.repeat_search_changes: A second, more careful search of the car reveals faint wipe-marks on the steering wheel and door handle inconsistent with normal use, prompting the question of who else might have driven it

locations.name: Kestrel Cannery Outflow Dock (abandoned)
locations.description: A crumbling, half-collapsed dock structure at the mouth of the old cannery's discharge channel, a mile up the shore road from town, rarely visited and unlit at night.
searchable_objects: Loose shoreline stones (identical in kind to the murder weapon, none individually identifiable)
A faint drag mark in the mud near the water's edge
possible_tests: Tide/algae-line comparison to determine where a body entered the water
Soil/mud composition comparison to trace found on the victim's clothing
hidden_items: A distinct algae staining line on nearby rocks that, cross-referenced with tide charts, indicates the water level and likely point of entry at approximately 19:20-19:40 on November 3rd - matching mud composition later found on Tom's trouser cuffs, which does not match the town dock's mud composition
locations.repeat_search_changes: Only searched at all once investigators begin questioning the town-dock staging; yields the case's most decisive circumstantial finding once examined

locations.name: The Grey Harbor Beacon office
locations.description: A cramped two-room newspaper office above the hardware store, run by Tom and Priya for over a decade.
searchable_objects: His computer (password-protected, unlocked via IT recovery)
possible_tests: Cloud backup recovery of deleted or synced drafts
hidden_items: Tom's cloud-synced draft email outlining 'name change filed 1994' and 'relief fund - who actually controls it now?' - the single most important documentary lead in the case, requiring a warrant or Priya's consent to access
locations.repeat_search_changes: A second, technically assisted search (IT forensic recovery) surfaces the cloud draft that a manual search of the physical office would never find, since his physical notes were stolen

locations.name: Grey Harbor Public Library, local history room
locations.description: A small room of bound old newspapers, county records microfilm, and donated historical materials.
searchable_objects: Microfilm reels of 1979 Beacon issues covering the cannery closure

crime_scene.location: Officially discovered at LOC1 (Town Dock); actually occurred at LOC2 (Kestrel Cannery Outflow Dock)
crime_scene.condition_on_discovery: Tom Ashby's body was found floating against the pilings near the town dock at dawn on November 4th, his car parked nearby as though he had gone there to write, as was his habit. No phone, recorder, or satchel were found on him or in the car.
crime_scene.initial_assumption: Accidental drowning after a nighttime fall from the dock, consistent with his known habits and the fog and dark conditions that night
crime_scene.actual_nature: A homicide that occurred a mile away, staged to look like it happened at his usual, expected spot
crime_scene.key_scene_contradiction: Tide charts and algae staining prove the water level and mud composition at the town dock do not match what is found on the body's clothing, while both precisely match conditions at the cannery outflow dock at the estimated time of death - meaning the body, or at minimum the vehicle, was moved after the fact, since a truly accidental fall at the town dock could never produce that particular staining pattern.

autopsy.cause_of_death: Drowning, with water present in the lungs consistent with the victim being alive upon entering the water
autopsy.time_of_death_estimate: 19:00-20:00 on 2025-11-03, based on stomach contents, water temperature, and body condition at discovery
additional_findings: A single curved, smooth-surfaced contusion on the left parietal region of the skull, sufficient to cause unconsciousness but survivable on its own

The contusion's shape is inconsistent with the town dock's square-edged timber pilings and inconsistent with any structure at the cannery outflow dock as well - consistent instead with a smooth, rounded handheld object
Defensive-type abrasions on both hands, consistent with a brief physical struggle immediately before the head injury
No alcohol or drugs in his system

Mud and algae composition on the trouser cuffs and shoes does not match the town dock's shoreline composition, but does match the cannery outflow dock's composition when independently sampled and compared
autopsy.conclusion: Death resulted from unconsciousness caused by a deliberate blow with a rounded object, followed by drowning while incapacitated, at a location different from where the body and vehicle were later found - conclusively establishing homicide with a staged discovery scene.

forensics.finding: Curved, smooth wound pattern inconsistent with either dock's structural surfaces, consistent with a handheld rounded stone or similar object
Matches the cannery outflow dock's shoreline sediment, not the town dock's
forensics.plausibility_note: Comparative soil/sediment forensic analysis, an established technique

forensics.finding: Water level and algae-line staining at the outflow dock are consistent with body/clothing contact occurring between 19:20-19:40 that evening
forensics.plausibility_note: Straightforward application of tide tables and shoreline staining analysis

forensics.item: Cell tower data (Tom's phone, before it went dark)
forensics.finding: Last activity pings a tower consistent with the cannery outflow road at 18:55, not the town dock

Faint wipe-marks on the steering wheel and door handle inconsistent with normal use patterns; absence of expected water/mud transfer consistent with a driver who was not soaked, suggesting someone other than Tom drove it to the town dock afterward
forensics.plausibility_note: Reasonable trace-evidence and wear-pattern inference, appropriately treated as suggestive rather than individually conclusive

forensics.finding: Cash purchase three days before the murder, times and matches the anonymous call placed to Tom's phone
Consistent facial correspondence between a present-day photo of Warren Pell and the 1979 badge photo of teenage Warren Pelletier, supported by the legal filing itself
forensics.plausibility_note: Documentary record correlation supported by a professional facial-comparison opinion, appropriately treated as strong corroboration rather than an infallible match

forensics.finding: Thirty years of underpayment relative to documented principal and reasonable interest accrual, with Warren Pell as sole administrator

timeline.event: Tom leaves a voicemail with the County Records Office requesting 1979 Kestrel Cannery employment and name-change records.
Tom saves a cloud-synced draft outline noting 'name change filed 1994' and 'relief fund - who actually controls it now?'
An anonymous caller using a burner phone offers Tom original 1979 cannery documents, proposing a meeting at the cannery outflow dock the following evening.
Light drizzle over Grey Harbor.
Tom calls Priya Deshmukh, mentions 'one more thread to pull.'
Tom texts Priya: 'Heading out. If this checks out, we run it Thursday.'
Dense fog rolls in off the harbor.
Tom leaves his house, driving north out of town toward the cannery access road, calendar noting 'Outflow - 7pm - bring recorder.'
Tom's phone last pings a cell tower consistent with the cannery outflow road.
Warren Pell, having left his pantry delivery van near the outflow road (seen by neighbor Ida Marsh, who assumes a routine delivery run), waits near the outflow dock.
Reverend Elias Cho arrives at the county lockup to see his son (unrelated to the murder).
Denise Okafor-Hale leaves the Select Board meeting early.
Tom arrives at the cannery outflow dock and meets Warren, expecting to receive documents.
A confrontation occurs; it becomes clear to Warren that Tom already has enough information to identify his true family connection. A struggle breaks out over Tom's satchel.
Caleb Ashby buys canned goods with cash at a store near the family cabin, well outside Grey Harbor (unrelated to the murder).
Warren strikes Tom once with a smooth river stone; Tom falls unconscious into the tidal channel and drowns. Tide/algae evidence later anchors this window precisely.
Denise Okafor-Hale is seated at a restaurant in Aldermere (unrelated to the murder).
Warren takes Tom's phone, recorder, and satchel, and discards the murder weapon into the deep channel.

Warren drives Tom's car (using keys taken from his coat) from the outflow area to the town dock, wipes surfaces he touched inside it, and stages the scene to resemble Tom's usual nighttime writing spot.
Warren walks roughly a mile back along the shore road to retrieve his own pantry delivery van, left near the outflow road.
Fog persists over the harbor; light drizzle continues.
Lobsterman Hollis Baird spots Tom's body caught against the pilings near the town dock at dawn.
Sheriff's deputies arrive on scene, find Tom's car parked nearby, and note the absence of his phone, recorder, and satchel.
The body is transported to the county Medical Examiner's office in Aldermere.

In an informal conversation with Deputy Sarah Kwan, days before the Medical Examiner's report is released, Warren Pell remarks that Tom 'must have hit his head on the dock pilings' - a detail not yet public.

The Medical Examiner's report is completed and released to the sheriff's office only, confirming the skull contusion is inconsistent with the town dock's pilings; the report is not made public at this stage.

The 1994 name-change filing and 1979 badge photo

Warren_Pell.breaking_point: When shown the 1979 badge photo alongside the 1994 name-change filing, and asked to explain the relief fund's thirty-year shortfall, Warren's composure finally breaks.
Warren_Pell.final_admission_summary: Warren admits to his true identity and to administering, and substantially diverting, the relief fund for decades. Regarding the killing itself, he insists he only meant to talk Tom out of publishing, that the meeting 'got out of hand' when Tom recognized him and reached for his satchel, and that he 'never meant for him to go in the water' - stopping short of admitting the blow was struck with clear intent to kill, though the physical evidence and the deliberate staging afterward establish it as murder regardless of his characterization.

hidden_truth.full_narrative: In 1979, the Kestrel Cannery's wastewater discharge sickened several families along the Sallow River's tidal flats. Plant supervisor Arnold Pelletier, facing potential ruin, quietly negotiated a private settlement with the most vocal affected families rather than let the matter reach a courtroom or the press, and moved his family out of state within the year. His teenage son, Warren, absorbed both the shame of the cover-up and, eventually, control of the settlement fund itself after his parents' deaths. In 1994, Warren returned to Grey Harbor under his mother's maiden name, Pell, and spent three decades quietly rebuilding himself as one of the town's most trusted figures - church organist, food pantry director, a soft-spoken presence everyone confided in. He continued making the relief fund's payments personally, in cash, to the aging tidal-flat families, always with a gentle request for discretion - a request that let him monitor the story's containment indefinitely, while he steadily diverted a significant share of the fund's value for his own benefit over the years, a fraud layered directly on top of his father's original crime. Tom Ashby's eight-month investigation into the 1979 closure - begun as ordinary local history for the paper - led him to request old employment and name-change records that would eventually connect Warren Pell to Warren Pelletier, and from there to the relief fund's true, uninspected finances. Sensing exposure closing in, Warren contacted Tom anonymously using a prepaid phone, offering original 1979 documents in exchange for a meeting at the isolated cannery outflow dock after dark - a location and time chosen specifically because no camera or casual passerby would ever be present. When Tom arrived, it became clear during their conversation that he already possessed enough to identify Warren regardless of any documents on offer; a struggle broke out over Tom's satchel, and Warren, in a moment of panic rather than long premeditated intent to kill (though the meeting itself was very much premeditated), struck him once with a stone from the shoreline. Tom fell into the tidal channel, unconscious but alive, and drowned before Warren did anything to help him. Warren took the phone, recorder, and satchel to erase Tom's physical research, drove Tom's own car to the town dock to invoke the far more mundane and expected story of an accidental fall at his usual writing spot, wiped what he'd touched, and discarded the stone into deep water on his way back. He then walked back along the shore road to his own van, which a neighbor noticed and dismissed as an ordinary pantry delivery. In the days that followed, Warren was never treated as a serious suspect - he had no known conflict with Tom, a spotless reputation, and was, if anything, one of the more comforting, helpful presences around other suspects and witnesses during the investigation. His only real error was an entirely human one: mentioning, in passing, a detail about how Tom must have died that no public statement had yet described, because it was the detail from the story he himself had staged.

why_every_suspect_lied.Grady_Voss: Made an angry, hyperbolic threat in public out of genuine fear for his livelihood, unrelated to any actual intent to harm Tom
why_every_suspect_lied.Denise_Okafor_Hale: Concealed an unrelated ethics violation (a personal land investment ahead of a public vote) and a private business meeting, unrelated to the murder
why_every_suspect_lied.Reverend_Elias_Cho: Concealed a family crisis (his son's arrest and bail) and an unauthorized use of church funds, out of personal shame, unrelated to the murder
why_every_suspect_lied.Priya_Deshmukh: Concealed an ongoing breach of her partnership agreement (continued sale negotiations against Tom's wishes), unrelated to the murder, and had no need to lie about her alibi since it was always true
why_every_suspect_lied.Caleb_Ashby: Concealed minor illegal squatting and poaching out of fear of further legal trouble, unrelated to the murder
why_every_suspect_lied.Warren_Pell: Concealed both a minor, sympathetic theft (donation box funds for his wife's medical bills) and, far more significantly, his entire true identity and thirty years of financial fraud against the very families his fund was meant to help - the second concealment being the actual motive for murder

hidden_truth.why_every_red_herring_exists: Grey Harbor is a small, financially strained town where nearly every prominent figure is managing some private shame, debt, or impropriety; Tom's death, and his general reputation for uncomfortable reporting, meant that virtually anyone he'd recently crossed looked briefly plausible. The true killer, by contrast, was someone with no publicly visible conflict with Tom at all - which is precisely what allowed him to remain unexamined until the investigation ran out of louder alternatives and was forced to look instead at the physical geography of the death itself.
exact_reasoning_path_required_to_solve_t: 1. Establish, through autopsy and mud/algae composition, that the death did not occur where the body and car were found - the town dock scene was staged.
2. Use tide charts and cell-tower data to relocate the true time and place of death to the isolated cannery outflow dock.
3. Recognize that Tom went there voluntarily, which requires finding out who summoned him and why - leading to the burner phone and the anonymous documents offer.

4. Recover Tom's own research trail (cloud-synced notes, calendar entry, records office voicemail) to learn he was investigating a 1979 name change connected to the cannery scandal, redirecting suspicion away from the six suspects' obvious present-day conflicts and toward a hidden historical identity.

5. Cross-reference the 1979 employee badge photo archive with 1994 county name-change filings to identify Warren Pelletier as Warren Pell - a connection invisible without deliberately pursuing Tom's own research direction rather than the more obvious suspects' motives.
6. Audit the relief fund Warren privately controls to establish ongoing financial motive independent of, and far more serious than, his admitted minor donation-box theft.

7. Recognize the significance of Warren's offhand 'dock pilings' remark only by comparing it against the Medical Examiner's actual report and its release timeline, proving he could not have known that detail innocently.

8. Only with all of the above converging - none sufficient alone - does an accusation of Warren Pell become evidentially supportable, despite the complete absence of any single decisive forensic match, confession, or camera image.

player_progress.suggested_minimum_progress_before_accusa: 70 percent of available evidence/actions explored, including at minimum: town_dock_staging_identified, outflow_dock_discovered_as_true_scene, warren_true_identity_established, relief_fund_audited, and dock_pilings_slip_recognized

game_state_template.win_condition: Player accuses the correct suspect after having independently discovered the town-dock staging, the true outflow-dock crime scene, the killer's concealed true identity, the relief-fund fraud, and the significance of the unscripted scene-detail slip - not merely a lucky early guess.
game_state_template.lose_condition: Player accuses any incorrect suspect, or accuses the correct suspect without having assembled the required convergence of circumstantial evidence, which the system should flag as an unsupported accusation regardless of whether the identity guessed happens to be correct.
